stem: What is the difference between "distance" and "displacement"?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Distance is the total length of the path traveled (scalar); displacement is the straight-line change in position (vector)
choices.explanation: Distance is a scalar measuring total path length; displacement is a vector measuring the net change in position.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are always exactly the same value, since both measure how far the object has moved along its path
choices.explanation: They are equal only when motion is in a straight line with no reversal in direction; in general they differ.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Distance is a vector and displacement is a scalar, so only distance has a direction attached to it
choices.explanation: This reverses the correct classification -- distance is the scalar, displacement is the vector.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Displacement is always greater than distance, since it includes the direction of motion as well as length
choices.explanation: Displacement's magnitude is never greater than distance traveled; it can be equal to or less than it.

explanation: Distance is the total scalar path length traveled; displacement is the vector representing the net change in position.

stem: A runner jogs 300 m east, then turns around and jogs 100 m west. What is the magnitude of the runner's total displacement?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Net displacement = 300 m east - 100 m west = 200 m east; magnitude is 200 m.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the total distance traveled (300+100), not the net displacement.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This ignores the 100 m walked back west, which partially cancels the eastward displacement.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This only accounts for the return leg, not the net effect of both legs of the trip.

explanation: Displacement is a vector sum: 300 m east minus 100 m west leaves a net 200 m east.

stem: An object's position changes from $x = 2$ m to $x = 10$ m over a time interval of 4 s. What is its average velocity?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Average velocity = Δx/Δt = (10-2)/4 = 8/4 = 2 m/s.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the displacement (8 m) alone, not divided by the time interval.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides the time by the displacement rather than displacement by time.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly compute Δx/Δt using the given position and time values.

explanation: Average velocity is the displacement divided by the elapsed time: (10-2)/4 = 2 m/s.

stem: A car drives 100 m east, then immediately 100 m west, in a total time of 20 s. What are the car's average speed and average velocity, respectively?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Average speed = 10 m/s; average velocity = 0 m/s
choices.explanation: Average speed = total distance/time = 200/20 = 10 m/s. Average velocity = net displacement/time = 0/20 = 0 m/s, since the car returns to its starting point.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Average speed = 0 m/s; average velocity = 10 m/s
choices.explanation: This swaps the two results -- speed (using total distance) is 10 m/s, while velocity (using net displacement) is 0.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Average speed = 5 m/s; average velocity = 5 m/s
choices.explanation: Neither of these matches the correct total-distance or net-displacement calculation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Average speed = 10 m/s; average velocity = 10 m/s
choices.explanation: The average velocity is not 10 m/s; since the car returns to where it started, its net displacement -- and thus average velocity -- is zero.

explanation: Average speed uses total distance (200 m/20 s = 10 m/s); average velocity uses net displacement (0 m/20 s = 0 m/s).

stem: What does "instantaneous velocity" refer to?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The velocity of an object at a single specific moment in time
choices.explanation: Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at one specific instant, as opposed to averaged over an interval.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The velocity averaged over the entire trip, from start to finish
choices.explanation: This describes average velocity, not instantaneous velocity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The maximum velocity reached at any time during the motion
choices.explanation: Instantaneous velocity refers to velocity at a given moment, not specifically the maximum value reached.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The velocity only at the very end of the motion, at the final instant
choices.explanation: Instantaneous velocity can be evaluated at any moment, not just the final one.

explanation: Instantaneous velocity is an object's velocity at one specific moment in time.

stem: An object's velocity changes from 5 m/s to 15 m/s over a time interval of 4 s. What is its average acceleration?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Average acceleration = Δv/Δt = (15-5)/4 = 10/4 = 2.5 m/s².

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the change in velocity (10 m/s) alone, not divided by the time interval.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides the time by the velocity change rather than velocity change by time.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly compute Δv/Δt using the given velocity and time values.

explanation: Average acceleration is Δv/Δt: (15-5)/4 = 2.5 m/s².

stem: Can an object have a negative acceleration while speeding up?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes -- if the object moves in the negative direction, a negative acceleration (in the same direction as the velocity) increases its speed
choices.explanation: Sign only indicates direction; acceleration in the same direction as velocity always increases speed, regardless of the sign convention chosen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No -- negative acceleration always means the object is slowing down, whatever the direction of its motion or the sign of its velocity in every case
choices.explanation: This is a common misconception -- "negative" just means the acceleration vector points in the negative direction, which speeds up an object already moving in that direction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No -- acceleration can never be negative under any circumstances, because it measures only the size of a change
choices.explanation: Acceleration is a vector and its sign simply reflects direction relative to the chosen positive axis; it can absolutely be negative.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes, but only if the object is momentarily at rest at the moment the acceleration is measured
choices.explanation: This isn't a necessary condition -- an object already moving in the negative direction speeds up under negative acceleration regardless of whether it was ever at rest.

explanation: An object speeds up whenever its acceleration points in the same direction as its velocity -- regardless of whether that direction is labeled positive or negative.

stem: On a position-vs-time graph, what does the slope at any point represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The instantaneous velocity at that point
choices.explanation: The slope of a position-time graph, dx/dt, is by definition the instantaneous velocity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The instantaneous acceleration at that point
choices.explanation: Acceleration is the slope of a VELOCITY-time graph, not a position-time graph.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Total distance isn't read directly from the slope of a position-time graph.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Mass has no relationship to the slope of a position-time graph.

explanation: The slope of a position-time graph represents instantaneous velocity.

stem: On a velocity-vs-time graph, what does the slope at any point represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The instantaneous acceleration at that point
choices.explanation: The slope of a velocity-time graph, dv/dt, is by definition the instantaneous acceleration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The instantaneous velocity at that point on the graph
choices.explanation: Velocity is read directly from the vertical axis value, not the slope, of a velocity-time graph.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The total displacement of the object
choices.explanation: Displacement is the AREA under a velocity-time graph, not its slope.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The object's position at that moment
choices.explanation: Position isn't directly represented by the slope of a velocity-time graph.

explanation: The slope of a velocity-time graph represents instantaneous acceleration.

stem: On a velocity-vs-time graph, what does the area under the curve between two times represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The displacement of the object during that time interval
choices.explanation: The area under a velocity-time graph equals the definite integral of velocity, which is displacement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The acceleration of the object at the end of that interval
choices.explanation: Acceleration is the SLOPE of a velocity-time graph, not the area under it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mass of the object being measured
choices.explanation: Mass has no relationship to the area under a velocity-time graph.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The maximum velocity reached during the interval
choices.explanation: The maximum velocity would be read directly from the graph's peak height, not the area under it.

explanation: The area under a velocity-time graph equals the object's displacement over that interval.

stem: The position-time graph below shows an object's motion. During which time interval is the object's velocity zero?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The graph is flat (zero slope) from t=2s to t=5s, meaning velocity is zero -- the object is at rest during this interval.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The graph has a positive, nonzero slope during this interval (position rises from 0 to 10 m), so velocity is nonzero here.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The object's velocity is never zero
choices.explanation: The flat segment from t=2s to t=5s does have zero slope, meaning the velocity is zero during that interval.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The object's velocity is zero for the entire graph
choices.explanation: The velocity is nonzero (positive) during the first segment, t=0 to t=2s, where position is increasing.

explanation: The flat segment (zero slope) from t=2s to t=5s indicates the object's velocity is zero -- it has stopped moving.

diagram.altText: Position-time graph rising from 0 to 10 meters between t=0 and t=2 seconds, then flat at 10 meters from t=2 to t=5 seconds

stem: The velocity-time graph below shows an object accelerating uniformly from rest. What is the object's total displacement between t=0 and t=4 s?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Displacement = area under the graph = area of the triangle = (1/2)(base)(height) = (1/2)(4)(8) = 16 m.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the final velocity value, not the area under the graph (displacement).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is double the correct area -- forgetting the (1/2) factor for a triangular region.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is the acceleration (slope), not the displacement (area).

explanation: Displacement equals the area under the v-t graph: a triangle with base 4 s and height 8 m/s, giving (1/2)(4)(8) = 16 m.

diagram.altText: Velocity-time graph rising in a straight line from 0 to 8 meters per second between t=0 and t=4 seconds

stem: The velocity-time graph below shows an object's motion. What is the object's acceleration between t=2 s and t=5 s?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The graph is flat (zero slope) from t=2s to t=5s, meaning velocity is constant at 6 m/s -- so acceleration is zero.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the acceleration during the FIRST segment (t=0 to t=2s), not the flat segment asked about.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the constant velocity value during that interval, not the acceleration (slope).

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly read the slope of the flat segment, which is zero.

explanation: From t=2s to t=5s the graph is flat (constant velocity), so the slope -- and thus the acceleration -- is zero.

diagram.altText: Velocity-time graph rising from 0 to 6 meters per second between t=0 and t=2 seconds, then flat at 6 meters per second from t=2 to t=5 seconds

stem: A velocity-time graph shows a horizontal line at $v = 0$ for a time interval. What does this indicate about the object during that interval?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The object is at rest (not moving)
choices.explanation: A velocity of zero means the object isn't moving during that interval -- it's stationary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The object is moving at constant, nonzero speed
choices.explanation: A horizontal line at v=0 specifically indicates zero velocity, not a nonzero constant speed.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A horizontal (flat) line indicates zero acceleration (no change in velocity), not rapid acceleration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The object's position is changing rapidly
choices.explanation: With zero velocity, the object's position is NOT changing at all during this interval.

explanation: A horizontal line at v=0 on a velocity-time graph means the object is at rest during that interval.

stem: The position-time graph below shows an object's motion from t=0 to t=4 s. What does this graph indicate about the object's motion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The object moves at a constant velocity of -2 m/s (in the negative direction)
choices.explanation: The graph is a straight line with constant negative slope: (2-10)/(4-0) = -8/4 = -2 m/s, indicating constant velocity in the negative direction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The object is speeding up in the positive direction as time passes, covering more distance each second
choices.explanation: The position is DECREASING (not increasing), and the slope is constant (not curving), so this doesn't describe the motion shown.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The object is at rest for the entire interval, at a fixed position
choices.explanation: The position changes continuously from 10 m to 2 m, so the object is clearly moving, not at rest.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The object's velocity is increasing over time, curving upward
choices.explanation: The graph is a straight line, meaning the slope (velocity) is CONSTANT throughout, not increasing.

explanation: The straight-line graph has a constant slope of -2 m/s, indicating constant velocity in the negative direction.

diagram.altText: Position-time graph falling in a straight line from 10 meters to 2 meters between t=0 and t=4 seconds

stem: An object starts from rest and accelerates at $3 \text{ m/s}^2$ for 4 seconds. What is its final velocity?

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is just the acceleration value, not multiplied by the time elapsed.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly compute v0+at using the given acceleration and time.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides time by acceleration rather than multiplying acceleration by time.

explanation: Using v = v0 + at: v = 0 + (3)(4) = 12 m/s.

stem: A car moving at 10 m/s decelerates at $2 \text{ m/s}^2$ for 3 seconds. What is its velocity at the end of this time?

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly subtract the full (2)(3)=6 m/s velocity change from the initial 10 m/s.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This incorrectly ADDS the velocity change rather than subtracting it, despite the car decelerating.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This overshoots into a reversed direction; the car hasn't decelerated enough to actually reverse direction in this scenario.

explanation: Using v = v0 + at with a=-2 m/s²: v = 10 + (-2)(3) = 4 m/s.

stem: An object starts at $x_0 = 0$ with an initial velocity of 5 m/s and accelerates at $2 \text{ m/s}^2$. What is its position after 3 seconds?

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This only accounts for the constant-velocity term (v0t), omitting the acceleration term entirely.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This only accounts for the acceleration term, omitting the initial-velocity contribution (v0t).

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly apply the (1/2) factor in the acceleration term of the kinematic equation.

stem: An object starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at $4 \text{ m/s}^2$. How far has it traveled after 5 seconds?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: x = (1/2)at^2 = (0.5)(4)(25) = 50 m (v0=0 removes the first term).

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This omits the (1/2) factor and doesn't correctly square the time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is double the correct value -- omitting the (1/2) factor in the kinematic equation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly apply x=(1/2)at² with the given acceleration and time.

stem: A car traveling at 20 m/s brakes with a constant deceleration of $4 \text{ m/s}^2$. How long does it take to stop?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Using v=v0+at with v=0: 0 = 20 + (-4)t, so t = 20/4 = 5 s.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly divide the initial velocity by the magnitude of deceleration.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly apply v=v0+at to solve for the stopping time.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This incorrectly multiplies rather than divides the given values.

explanation: Setting v=0 in v=v0+at: 0 = 20 - 4t, so t = 5 s.

stem: An object starts from rest and accelerates at $2 \text{ m/s}^2$. Using $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$, how far has it traveled once it reaches a velocity of 10 m/s?

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is double the correct answer -- omitting the factor of 2 in the denominator (2a).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly square the velocity or divide by 2a.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is just the velocity value, not the correctly computed distance.

explanation: Solving v²=v0²+2aΔx for Δx: Δx = 100/(2·2) = 25 m.

stem: An object is dropped from rest and falls freely under gravity ($g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$). What is its velocity after falling for 2 seconds?

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is just g itself, not multiplied by the 2-second fall time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides g by the time rather than multiplying.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is double the correct velocity, likely from multiplying by 4 instead of 2.

stem: An object is dropped from rest from a height of 44.1 m ($g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$). How long does it take to hit the ground?

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly solve h=(1/2)gt² for t using the given height.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is t² itself, not the square root needed to find t.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly apply the free-fall height equation to solve for time.

explanation: Solving h=(1/2)gt² for t: t² = 2(44.1)/9.8 = 9, so t = 3 s.

stem: For a projectile launched with some horizontal velocity (ignoring air resistance), how are its horizontal and vertical motions related?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are independent of each other: horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical motion has free-fall acceleration
choices.explanation: In projectile motion, horizontal and vertical motions are independent: horizontal velocity is constant (no horizontal force), while vertical motion accelerates due to gravity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are always equal in magnitude at every instant of the flight, so the two velocities match
choices.explanation: The horizontal and vertical velocity components are generally different and change independently over the course of the flight.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Horizontal motion also accelerates due to gravity, at the same rate as the vertical motion
choices.explanation: Gravity acts only vertically (ignoring air resistance); it does not affect horizontal motion, which stays at constant velocity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vertical motion stops as soon as horizontal motion begins, so the object moves in a straight line
choices.explanation: Both motions occur simultaneously throughout the flight; vertical motion doesn't stop when horizontal motion is present.

explanation: Horizontal and vertical motions in projectile motion are independent: horizontal velocity is constant, vertical motion accelerates under gravity.

stem: A ball rolls off a table with a horizontal velocity of 10 m/s and falls a height of 19.6 m to the ground ($g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2$). How long does it take to hit the ground?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Using h=(1/2)gt^2 (vertical motion only): 19.6=(0.5)(9.8)t^2, so t^2=4, t=2 s.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly solve the free-fall height equation for time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly account for the full 19.6 m height in the free-fall equation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is double the correct time -- likely from an error taking the square root of t²=4.

explanation: The fall time depends only on the vertical motion: t² = 2(19.6)/9.8 = 4, so t = 2 s.

stem: Using the same scenario -- a ball rolls off a table with a horizontal velocity of 10 m/s and takes 2 s to hit the ground -- how far horizontally does the ball travel before landing?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Horizontal motion is at constant velocity: x = v0x·t = (10)(2) = 20 m.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is just the horizontal velocity, not multiplied by the 2-second flight time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the given fall height, not the horizontal distance traveled.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides rather than multiplies the horizontal velocity by the flight time.

explanation: Horizontal distance = horizontal velocity × time = (10)(2) = 20 m.

stem: A ball is launched at 25 m/s at an angle of 37° above the horizontal ($\sin 37° \approx 0.6$, $\cos 37° \approx 0.8$). What are the horizontal and vertical components of its initial velocity?

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This swaps the sine and cosine components -- the horizontal component uses cosine (0.8), giving 20, not 15.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This doesn't apply the sine/cosine decomposition at all -- both components can't equal the full magnitude.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This assumes a 45° angle (equal components), not the actual 37° angle given.

stem: Using the same launch as before ($v_{0x}=20$ m/s, $v_{0y}=15$ m/s, $g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2$), and assuming the ball lands at the same height it was launched from, what is its total time of flight?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Time of flight (level launch/landing) = 2v0y/g = 2(15)/9.8 ≈ 3.06 s.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is half the correct time -- it's the time to reach maximum height only, not the full time of flight.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly apply the time-of-flight formula 2v0y/g.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is double the correct time of flight.

explanation: Time of flight = 2v0y/g = 2(15)/9.8 ≈ 3.06 s.

stem: Using the same launch ($v_{0y}=15$ m/s, $g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2$), what is the maximum height reached by the ball?

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is just the initial vertical velocity value, not the correctly computed max height.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is double the correct max height -- omitting the factor of 2 in the denominator.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly square the vertical velocity component in the max-height formula.

explanation: Max height = v0y²/(2g) = 225/19.6 ≈ 11.5 m.

stem: Using the same launch ($v_{0x}=20$ m/s, time of flight ≈ 3.06 s), what is the ball's horizontal range?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Range = v0x × time of flight = 20 × 3.06 ≈ 61.2 m.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is half the correct range.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is just the horizontal velocity, not multiplied by the time of flight.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is double the correct range.

explanation: Range = v0x × time of flight = 20 × 3.06 ≈ 61.2 m.
